text: Johnson, therefore, declines to rest the judgment upon his own admiration, since that admiration might be only the taste of a single age and a single temper. He asks what time has done to the work. The writer whose fame hangs upon the fashion of his day, upon local customs, or upon the quarrels of a party, may be applauded while the fashion lasts; when the fashion has passed, the applause which lived by it passes also. Those works alone can be said to have proved their worth which continue to please readers who inherit none of the circumstances of their first audience. Such readers bring no partiality to the trial; they have no friendship with the author, no concern in maintaining his opinions, and read him only because he still gives pleasure.
